meta.note: Regional timings come from climatology and past strong events (1997–98, 2015–16, 2023–24), laid over the current forecast. This is a risk map, not a weather forecast. Month indexes count from January 2026 (0) to December 2027 (23). conf: 3 = almost always seen in past strong events, 2 = often, 1 = sometimes.

nino34.note: Schematic. Only September 2026 (+2.1 °C, NOAA CPC monthly value) is an observed anchor; the rest is interpolation and an illustrative forecast spread.

items.name: Global temperature records
items.desc: Global temperature lags Niño-3.4 by 3–5 months. 2027 is likely to be the warmest year on record.
items.precedent: 1998, 2016 and 2024 were record years right after the peak

items.name: Mass coral bleaching
items.desc: Tropical marine heatwaves, especially in the southern hemisphere summer (Great Barrier Reef, Indian Ocean).

items.name: Food prices: rice, sugar, cocoa, coffee, palm oil
items.desc: Several regions lose harvests at once. Prices react to expectations before the harvests themselves.
items.precedent: Cocoa and rice price spikes in 2023–24

items.name: Peru and Ecuador: coastal downpours, mudslides
items.desc: Warm water off the coast brings rain to a normally dry desert. Mudslides, broken roads, dengue. Peaks in February–March.
items.precedent: 1998: about $3bn of damage in Peru; 2017 coastal El Niño

items.name: Peru: anchovy catch collapse
items.desc: Warm water pushes fish deeper and south. Fishing seasons are cut or cancelled, which hits the world fishmeal market.

items.name: Central America Dry Corridor: drought
items.desc: The July–August dry spell (canícula) ruins maize and bean crops in Guatemala, Honduras, El Salvador and Nicaragua.
items.precedent: 2015 and 2023: crop failure and more migration

items.name: Panama Canal: low water
items.desc: A dry season after a rainfall deficit lowers Gatún Lake. Limits on draft and on the number of transits.
items.precedent: 2023–24: transits cut by about a third

items.name: Colombia and Venezuela: drought, hydropower shortfall
items.desc: A harsher dry season. Hydro-dependent grids run close to the limit; cities ration water.
items.precedent: 2016 power crisis; 2024 water rationing in Bogotá

items.name: Amazon: drought, low rivers, fires
items.desc: Rivers drop and cut off communities; fires and carbon emissions. Record-low river levels.
items.precedent: 2015–16 and 2023: record lows on the Rio Negro

items.name: Southern Brazil, Uruguay, northern Argentina: floods
items.desc: Two bursts: in spring (Oct–Dec) and autumn (Apr–Jun). Floods in Rio Grande do Sul, good soy harvests in Argentina.
items.precedent: May 2024 Rio Grande do Sul disaster

items.name: Atlantic hurricanes suppressed
items.desc: Wind shear over the Atlantic suppresses hurricanes. A rare upside of El Niño, and it is already behind us.

items.name: Southern US and Mexico: wet, cool winter
items.desc: The jet stream shifts south: rain and storms from Texas to Florida, and a winter tornado risk in Florida.

items.name: California: storms and landslides
items.desc: Atmospheric rivers are possible. The signal is unreliable.

items.name: Northern US and Canada: warm winter
items.desc: Little snow, weak ice on the Great Lakes. Good for heating bills, bad for winter tourism.

items.name: Ethiopia and Sudan: rainy-season drought
items.desc: Weak summer (kiremt) rains in northern Ethiopia. Crop losses show up in autumn.

items.name: East Africa: short-rains floods
items.desc: Kenya, Somalia, southern Ethiopia, Tanzania. Heavy Oct–Dec rains, especially with a positive Indian Ocean Dipole.

items.name: Cholera, malaria, Rift Valley fever after floods
items.desc: Standing water and broken sanitation after the East African floods.

items.name: Southern Africa: rainy-season drought
items.desc: Zimbabwe, Zambia, Malawi, Mozambique, South Africa, Madagascar. The rains fail at the critical time for maize.

items.name: Southern Africa: maize failure and hunger
items.desc: Harvest is in April–May and the shortfall shows at once, but the lean season runs October 2027 – March 2028. Kariba hydropower drops too.
items.precedent: 2024: Zambia, Zimbabwe and Malawi declared disasters

items.name: West Africa: cocoa
items.desc: A dry harmattan and heat reduce the crop in Côte d'Ivoire and Ghana. The El Niño link is weaker than in the south.

items.name: India: weak monsoon
items.desc: Historically about 60% of El Niño years had a rainfall deficit. 2026 outcomes are not checked here.

items.name: Indonesia and Malaysia: drought, fires, haze
items.desc: Peat fires and smog over Singapore and Malaysia. Ends when the monsoon arrives in November–December.
items.precedent: 2015: 2.6 million ha burned, hundreds of thousands sick

items.name: Palm oil: delayed yield drop
items.desc: The 2026 drought hits yields 6–24 months later, so the impact lands in 2027.

items.name: Philippines, Thailand, Vietnam, Mekong: drought
items.desc: A hard dry season: rice, sugar, robusta coffee, saltwater intrusion in the Mekong delta.

items.name: Southern China: wet winter
items.desc: More rain in southern and south-eastern China.
items.precedent: 1998: major Yangtze floods in the summer after the peak

items.name: South Asia: pre-monsoon heat 2027
items.desc: The year after El Niño often brings extreme heat in April–June.

items.name: Dengue in South-East Asia and Latin America
items.desc: Heat and standing water speed up mosquito breeding.

items.name: Eastern Australia: dry spring, grain losses
items.desc: Less winter and spring rain. Stronger signal with a positive Indian Ocean Dipole.

items.name: Australia: heat and bushfire season
items.desc: Vegetation dried out by spring, then summer heat.
items.precedent: 1982–83 and 2006 coincided with El Niño (2019–20 did not)

items.name: Western Pacific: drought, drinking-water shortage
items.desc: Papua New Guinea, Micronesia, Marshall Islands, Palau. Frost in the PNG highlands.
items.precedent: 1997–98 and 2015–16: hunger in the PNG highlands

items.name: Central Pacific: cyclones shift east
items.desc: Cyclones reach French Polynesia and Kiribati more often.
